questions.questionText: What mathematical rule is backpropagation fundamentally built on?
options: The chain rule from calculus, applied repeatedly from the output layer backward to earlier layers
questions.correctAnswer: The chain rule from calculus, applied repeatedly from the output layer backward to earlier layers
questions.explanation: Backpropagation computes each layer's gradient by multiplying the gradient from the layer after it by the local derivative at that layer — exactly the chain rule, applied systematically.

questions.questionText: Why is backpropagation computationally efficient for deep networks, rather than requiring separate work per layer?
options: It isn't efficient — deep networks are simply slow to train
Each layer's gradient calculation reuses the gradient already computed for the layer after it, rather than being re-derived from scratch
It only computes gradients for the first layer
It skips computing gradients for most weights
questions.correctAnswer: Each layer's gradient calculation reuses the gradient already computed for the layer after it, rather than being re-derived from scratch
questions.explanation: The chain rule application naturally reuses intermediate results as you move backward, which is exactly what makes a single backward pass sufficient to compute every weight's gradient.

questions.questionText: In the XOR example, why couldn't a single-layer model (like plain logistic regression) solve it, but a network with a hidden layer could?
options: XOR requires more training data than was provided
XOR isn't linearly separable, and a single layer can only learn a linear decision boundary — the hidden layer adds the nonlinearity needed
XOR can only be solved with convolutional layers
The learning rate was set incorrectly for the single-layer case
questions.correctAnswer: XOR isn't linearly separable, and a single layer can only learn a linear decision boundary — the hidden layer adds the nonlinearity needed
questions.explanation: This directly connects back to the earlier lesson: a single neuron is limited to linear boundaries, and XOR is the textbook example of a pattern that requires a nonlinear boundary to separate.
